explanation: 'Gives' is the main verb of the sentence.
'Extremely' modifies the adjective 'excited', functioning as an adverb of degree.
'Breakfast'/'cafe' are nouns naming things in the sentence.
'Heavy' describes the rucksack, functioning as an adjective.
'Yourself' is a reflexive pronoun.
'Yet' joins the two contrasting clauses, functioning as a conjunction.
'Expensive' describes the clothes, functioning as an adjective.
'Innocence' is an abstract noun, the subject of the sentence.
'Well' describes how Liana sings, functioning as an adverb of manner.
'For' completes the phrasal verb 'sent for' (to summon), functioning as a preposition.
'For two years' signals an action continuing to now, taking the present perfect continuous 'has been living'.
'At the moment' signals an action in progress, taking the present continuous 'are working'.
'Never...anymore' fits the present perfect 'have seen', describing an unbroken state up to now.
A habitual action with 'We' takes the simple present 'do'.
The passive construction 'is...after' requires the past participle 'sought' (sought after).
An action interrupted by a past simple event takes the past continuous 'was crying'.
'Since morning' signals an action continuing to now, taking the present perfect continuous 'have been waiting'.
'A week ago' is a definite past time marker, taking the simple past 'went'.
Describing a past state of the bags takes the simple past 'were'.
The present perfect of 'lay' (lay-laid-laid) is 'laid', giving 'has...laid'.
'Between' is used when dividing something among exactly two people.
The passive voice agent is introduced with 'by'.
'Besides' means 'in addition to', fitting the sense that a song was written in addition to the poems.
'At' is used for a specific point/place such as an airport.
'Since' is used with a specific starting point in time (Tuesday) for an ongoing state.
'Till' expresses working up to a point in time (the evening).
'Into' expresses motion ending inside an enclosed space, like a well.
'On foot' is the standard idiomatic phrase for walking somewhere.
'Fond of' is the standard collocation.
'True to' (one's promises) is the standard collocation.
'Will cry' is the simple future tense.
'Protested' is the simple past tense.
'Love' here expresses a general, habitual state, the simple present tense.
'Is crying' is the present continuous tense.
'Have finished' is the present perfect tense.
'Have been working...for six hours' is the present perfect continuous tense.
'Had not realized' is the past perfect tense.
'Eats' describes a habitual action, the simple present tense.
'Addressed' is the simple past tense.
'Will have learnt' is the future perfect tense.
The conditional conjunction 'if' combines the two sentences: 'If you wait long enough, you will get what you want.'
'Neither...nor' is the correct correlative pairing (unlike the ungrammatical 'neither...or'), giving 'Neither a lender nor a borrower be.'
'Paraphernalia' means equipment or belongings consisting of miscellaneous articles.
The Government of India constituted a Commission under Article 340 to examine sub-categorisation of OBCs in the central list (the Rohini Commission).
Article 335 provides for considering the claims of SC/ST candidates in appointments to services and posts.
Photons, being massless, travel at the speed of light; electrons, neutrons and muons all have mass and travel slower.
Preposition, noun and adverb are all parts of speech; 'punctuation' is not a part of speech at all, making it the odd one out.
